target_claim: For ANY edge f of T2 crossing the cut (A,B) induced by deleting e from T1, both (T1\{e})+{f} and (T2\{f})+{e} are trees. The second part is false for arbitrary crossing f.
source_quote:
there must exist at least one edge f in T2 that connects a vertex in A to
a vertex in B. Choose any such edge f.
test_sketch: Implement the stated procedure: given trees T1,T2 on V and e in T1, compute components A,B of T1\{e}, enumerate every f in T2 with one endpoint in A and one in B (the proof claims ANY such f works), and check with a brute-force is_tree oracle (connected + |edges|=n-1 via BFS) that (T2\{f})+{e} is a tree. Counterexample at n=4: T1 = {1-2,2-3,3-4}, e = {2,3} so A={1,2}, B={3,4}; T2 = star {1-2,1-3,1-4}. Crossing edge f={1,4} gives (T2\{f})+{e} = {1-2,1-3,2-3} with vertex 4 isolated and a triangle 1-2-3: not a tree. Randomized sweep over all tree pairs on n<=6 and all (e,f) crossing choices finds many such failures.
